title: Battered Sausage
subtitle: Pork sausage in crisp beer batter from the chip shop
excerpt: A battered sausage is a pork sausage dipped in beer batter and deep-fried until the batter is golden and crisp. It is one of the classic items on a British chip-shop menu, eaten with chips, salt, and malt vinegar. The batter should be light and bubbly, not thick and doughy.
sourceNotes: Battered and deep-fried fish and sausages have been sold in British fish-and-chip shops since the late nineteenth century. The battered sausage alongside chips became a staple chip-shop item in the twentieth century. Beer batter is the traditional British formula for fish and chips and carries over to the sausage version.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: Par-cook the sausages up to 2 hours ahead. Make the batter just before frying.

content.text: A battered sausage is a par-cooked pork sausage dipped in beer batter and deep-fried until the batter is pale gold and crisp. The beer batter is the same as for fish and chips: plain flour, baking powder, and cold beer whisked together. The carbonation in the beer creates the bubbles that give the batter its light, airy texture. The sausage must be pre-cooked before battering, as the frying time is only long enough to cook the batter, not raw meat.

Place {{sausages-pork}} of sausages in a frying pan over a medium heat with a splash of water. Cook for 12 to 15 minutes, turning regularly, until cooked through and lightly browned. Transfer to a plate and leave to cool for 10 minutes. The sausages need to be fully cooked at this stage; they will only be in the oil for 2 to 3 minutes.
Make the batter and heat the oil

Whisk {{plain-flour}} of plain flour, {{baking-powder}} of baking powder, and {{salt-table}} of salt together in a bowl. Pour in {{beer}} of cold beer and whisk until just smooth. Do not overmix; a few small lumps are fine. The batter should be the consistency of thick double cream. Refrigerate while the oil heats.
Pour the {{vegetable-oil}} of oil into a large, deep, heavy-based saucepan to a depth of at least 8 cm. Heat over a medium-high heat to 180°C. Use a thermometer; do not guess the temperature.

Pat the cooled sausages dry with kitchen paper. Holding a sausage by one end, dip it into the batter and let the excess drip off for a second. Lower carefully into the hot oil using tongs and release. Fry for 2 to 3 minutes, turning once, until the batter is golden all over. Do not fry more than two at a time or the oil temperature drops too far.
Lift out with tongs, drain briefly on kitchen paper, and serve immediately with chips, salt, and malt vinegar.

items.symptom: The batter falls off in the oil
items.cause: The sausage surface was wet, or the oil was not hot enough.
items.fix: Pat the sausages completely dry before dipping. Check the oil temperature with a thermometer; below 175°C the batter does not set immediately and slides off.

items.symptom: The batter is thick and doughy, not crisp
items.cause: Too much flour, or the oil was too cool.
items.fix: The batter should be pourable and the consistency of thick double cream. Add a splash more cold beer to loosen if it is too thick. Ensure the oil is at 180°C before frying.

items.symptom: The inside of the batter is gummy
items.cause: The sausage was still cold from the fridge and cooled the oil too rapidly.
items.fix: Always use par-cooked sausages at room temperature, not cold from the fridge. Cold food drops the oil temperature dramatically.

content.text: The battered sausage is a chip-shop item rather than a home-cooking standard, but it is straightforward to make at home if you are already frying chips. The sausage batter uses the same mix as fish and the method is identical; the difference is only the interior. In northern England the battered sausage has an especially devoted following. It is eaten with chips, salt, and malt vinegar, and sometimes ketchup or curry sauce depending on region. It is not the same as a corn dog, which uses cornmeal batter and fries on a stick; the British version uses wheat batter and is served cut open or whole.
